chunks.text: 2 Method Our objective is to improve the separation of adjacent cells in dense microscopy images by predicting a continuous signed distance function (SDF) and optimizing a differentiable Modified Hausdorff Distance–based loss, enabling precise boundary localization and reduced topological errors. Boundary-based Loss. The proposed boundary-based loss is derived from the Hausdorff distance. Let S GT : Ω → { 0 , 1 } S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\colon\Omega\to\{0,1\} and S PRED : Ω → { 0 , 1 } S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}\colon\Omega\to\{0,1\} denote the binary GT segmentation of a single cell instance and the predicted segmentation, respectively, where Ω ⊂ ℝ 2 \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is the entire image domain. Each segmentation mask can be represented as a set of pixels: ω GT ≜ { 𝐱 i } i = 1 M \omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\triangleq\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} , with 𝐱 i ∈ { Ω | S GT ​ ( 𝐱 i ) = 1 } \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\{\Omega\,|\,S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})=1\} , and ω PRED ≜ { 𝐲 j } j = 1 N \omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}\triangleq\{\mathbf{y}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} , with 𝐲 j ∈ { Ω | S PRED ​ ( 𝐲 j ) = 1 } \mathbf{y}_{j}\in\{\Omega\,|\,S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{y}_{j})=1\} . The cardinalities may differ, i.e., M ≜ | ω GT | ≠ N ≜ | ω PRED | M\triangleq|\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}|\neq N\triangleq|\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}| .

The classical Hausdorff distance is defined as: D H ( S GT , S PRED ) = max { \displaystyle D_{H}(S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}},S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}})=\max\Big\{ sup 𝐱 i ∈ ω GT inf 𝐲 j ∈ ω PRED d ​ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) , \displaystyle\sup_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}\inf_{\mathbf{y}_{j}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}d(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j}), (1) sup 𝐲 j ∈ ω PRED inf 𝐱 i ∈ ω GT d ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) } , \displaystyle\sup_{\mathbf{y}_{j}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}\inf_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}d(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j})\Big\}, where d ​ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) d(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j}) is the Euclidean distance between pixels 𝐱 i ∈ ω GT \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}} and 𝐲 j ∈ ω PRED \mathbf{y}_{j}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}} . Following [ Dubuisson94 ] , we adopt an MHD by replacing the maximum and supremum operations in Eq. ( 1 ) with summations: D MH ​ ( S GT , S PRED ) = \displaystyle D_{\mbox{\footnotesize{MH}}}(S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}},S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}})= ∑ 𝐱 i ∈ ω GT inf 𝐲 j ∈ ω PRED d ​ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}\inf_{\mathbf{y}_{j}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}d(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j}) (2) + ∑ 𝐲 j ∈ ω PRED inf 𝐱 i ∈ ω GT d ​ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) . \displaystyle+\sum_{\mathbf{y}_{j}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}\inf_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}d(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j}). In the spirit of [ riklin2014mhd ] , we reformulate Eq. ( 2 ) using SDFs. Let ∂ ω ⊂ Ω \partial\omega\subset\Omega denote the boundary of ω \omega , representing an object region. The corresponding SDF ϕ : Ω → ℝ \phi\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is defined as: ϕ ​ ( 𝐱 ) = { d E ​ ( 𝐱 , ∂ ω ) , 𝐱 ∈ ω , − d E ​ ( 𝐱 , ∂ ω ) , 𝐱 ∈ Ω ∖ ω , \phi(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}d_{E}(\mathbf{x},\partial\omega),&\mathbf{x}\in\omega,\\ -d_{E}(\mathbf{x},\partial\omega),&\mathbf{x}\in\Omega\setminus\omega,\end{cases} (3) where d E ​ ( ⋅ ) d_{E}(\cdot) is the Euclidean distance.

We assume ϕ ​ ( 𝐱 ) \phi(\mathbf{x}) is differentiable almost everywhere and satisfies the Eikonal equation | ∇ ϕ ​ ( 𝐱 ) | = 1 |\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x})|=1 . Let ϕ GT \phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}} and ϕ PRED \phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}} be the SDFs for the GT and predicted segmentations, respectively, with boundaries ∂ ω GT \partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}} and ∂ ω PRED \partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}} . The absolute value | ϕ GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) | |\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x})| is the minimal Euclidean distance between 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and the boundary of S GT S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}} . Integrating | ϕ GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) | |\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x})| over all 𝐱 ∈ ∂ ω PRED \mathbf{x}\in\partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}} corresponds to the left-hand term of Eq. ( 2 ), and integrating | ϕ PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) | |\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x})| over 𝐱 ∈ ∂ ω GT \mathbf{x}\in\partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}} corresponds to the right-hand term: D CMH ​ ( S GT , S PRED ) = \displaystyle D_{\mbox{\footnotesize{CMH}}}(S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}},S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}})= ∫ ∂ ω GT | ϕ S PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) | ​ 𝑑 s \displaystyle\int_{\partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}\big|\phi_{S_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}(\mathbf{x})\big|\,ds (4) + ∫ ∂ ω PRED | ϕ S GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) | ​ 𝑑 s . \displaystyle+\int_{\partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}}\big|\phi_{S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}}(\mathbf{x})\big|\,ds. where d ​ s ds denotes an infinitesimal curve (in 2D) element along the object boundary. In practice, we train a neural network to directly predict the SDF of the cell segmentation. To define a differentiable boundary-based loss in the spirit of Eq. ( 4 ), we use a parameterized sigmoid function: σ α , β ​ ( z ) = 1 1 + exp ⁡ ( − ( α ​ z + β ) ) , \sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\left(\alpha z+\beta\right)\right)}, (5) where α \alpha and β \beta are learnable parameters.

While ϕ PRED : Ω → ( − ∞ , ∞ ) \phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}\colon\Omega\to(-\infty,\infty) , σ α , β ​ ( ϕ PRED ) \sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}) maps pixels to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , where each value can be interpreted as the probability of being inside the cell region. The predicted boundaries ∂ ω PRED \partial\omega_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}} are approximated by the differentiable soft boundary map: B PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) = σ α , β ​ ( ϕ PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) ​ σ α , β ​ ( − ϕ PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) , B_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x})=\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x}))\,\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(-\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x})), (6) and similarly for the GT boundaries: B GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) = σ α , β ​ ( ϕ GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) ​ σ α , β ​ ( − ϕ GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) . B_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x})=\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x}))\,\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(-\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x})). (7) Given the soft boundary maps’ formulation (Eq. 7 , Eq. 6 ), we define two MHD loss terms that discretize and approximate the left- and right-hand sides of Eq. ( 4 ). Since SDF values can be arbitrarily scaled in ℝ \mathbb{R} , we apply a hyperbolic tangent, which monotonically maps ( − ∞ , ∞ ) (-\infty,\infty) to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] : ℒ LMHD \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{LMHD}}} = ∑ 𝐱 ∈ Ω B GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ | tanh α , β ⁡ ( ϕ PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) | \displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega}B_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x})\,\big|\tanh_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x}))\big| (8) = B GT ⋅ | tanh PRED | . \displaystyle=B_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\cdot\big|\tanh_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}\big|. ℒ RMHD \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{RMHD}}} = ∑ 𝐱 ∈ Ω B PRED ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ | tanh α , β ⁡ ( ϕ GT ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) | \displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega}B_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}(\mathbf{x})\,\big|\tanh_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}(\mathbf{x}))\big| (9) = B PRED ⋅ | tanh GT | . \displaystyle=B_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}\cdot\big|\tanh_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\big|.

The parameterized hyperbolic tangent can be formulated by: tanh α , β ⁡ ( z ) = tanh ⁡ ( α ​ ( z − β ) ) = 2 ​ σ α , β ​ ( z ) − 1 . \tanh_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\tanh\big(\alpha(z-\beta)\big)=2\,\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(z)-1. (10) Unified loss function. Rather than predicting binary masks, our framework outputs continuous SDFs by using two additional loss terms. First, we introduce a Least Squares Error (LSE) loss between the predicted and ground-truth SDFs after applying the parameterized hyperbolic tangent: ℒ LSE = [ tanh α , β ⁡ ( ϕ PRED ) − tanh α , β ⁡ ( ϕ GT ) ] 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{LSE}}}=\left[\tanh_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}})-\tanh_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}})\right]^{2}. (11) Second, we define an SDF-based cross-entropy (CE) loss using the probabilistic interpretation of the predicted segmentation maps, i.e., σ α , β ​ ( ϕ PRED ) \sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}) : ℒ CE \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{CE}}} = − [ S GT log σ α , β ( ϕ PRED ) \displaystyle=-\Big[S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\,\log\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}}) (12) + ( 1 − S GT ) log ( 1 − σ α , β ( ϕ PRED ) ) ] . \displaystyle\quad+\big(1-S_{\mbox{\tiny{GT}}}\big)\log\big(1-\sigma_{\alpha,\beta}(\phi_{\mbox{\tiny{PRED}}})\big)\Big]. The final unified objective combines all four terms: ℒ Total = λ LMHD ​ ℒ LMHD + λ RMHD ​ ℒ RMHD + λ LSE ​ ℒ LSE + λ CE ​ ℒ CE , \mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{Total}}}=\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{LMHD}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{LMHD}}}+\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{RMHD}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{RMHD}}}+\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{LSE}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{LSE}}}+\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{CE}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mbox{\tiny{CE}}}, (13) where λ LMHD , λ RMHD , λ LSE , \lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{LMHD}}},\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{RMHD}}},\lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{LSE}}}, and λ CE \lambda_{\mbox{\tiny{CE}}} are weighting coefficients. For all experiments (except SAM) we used a U-Net backbone with feature widths {128, 256, 512, 1024} (approximately 49.7M learnable parameters) trained on 2D patches of size 128 × 128 128\times 128 with a batch size of 16. Standard augmentations—random affine transforms [ ronneberger2015unet ] , random crops, flips, and moderate brightness/contrast variations—are applied during training. The learnable sigmoid parameters are initialized as α = 4 \alpha{=}4 and β = 0 \beta{=}0 . Optimization uses AdamW with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\!\times\!10^{-4} and weight decay 1 × 10 − 3 1\!\times\!10^{-3} . The unified loss (Eq.

13 ) is weighted by λ LMHD = 0.9 \lambda_{\mathrm{LMHD}}{=}0.9 , λ RMHD = 10 − 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{RMHD}}{=}10^{-1} , λ LSE = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{LSE}}{=}1 , and λ CE = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}{=}1 . Training was performed on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU taking approximately 45 minutes per dataset including augmentation. Inference required on average 0.77 seconds per image. 3 Experiments and Results 3.1 Datasets Both public and private datasets were used for evaluation. CSB Dataset. For public data, we use four 2D sequences from the Cell Segmentation Benchmark (CSB) [ maska2014benchmark , maska2024csb , ulman2017ctc ] 2 2 2 https://celltrackingchallenge.net/ : Fluo-N2DH-SIM+, Fluo-N2DH-HeLa, Fluo-N2DH-GOWT1, and Fluo-C2DL-MSC, spanning challenging real fluorescence and brightfield imaging as well as high-throughput simulated data. Segmentations for the CSB datasets are provided as gold (expert-annotated, though partial) and silver masks, the latter obtained via label fusion of outputs from multiple top-performing algorithms. Spheroid Dataset. The private dataset was provided by the Lahav Lab and consists of 3D irradiated MCF7 human breast cancer spheroids acquired with Selective Plane Illumination Microscopy (SPIM) across five post-irradiation timepoints. This volumetric dataset contains densely packed nuclei, dynamic morphological changes, and heterogeneous p21 expression. Ground-truth segmentations were generated manually using napari 3 3 3 https://napari.org [ napari2023 ] . Preprocessing. Across all datasets, we remove 1-pixel-wide label borders introduced by annotation tools, while preserving all true cell regions and overlaps, to obtain clean instance separability for SDF computation. Training-test split. The CSB benchmark provides two annotated training sequences per dataset; We therefore trained on the first sequence and evaluated on the second.

For the 3D irradiated spheroid dataset, we used the manual 3D annotations to extract 539 labeled 2D slices, splitting them into 70% for training and 30% for testing, ensuring that slices from the same z-stack were not split across sets. 3.2 Evaluation Measure The SEG measure, introduced by the CSB organizers, quantifies segmentation accuracy as the mean Jaccard index between each ground-truth object and its best-matching predicted object where a prediction is considered a valid match to a ground-truth cell segmentation only if its intersection is higher than 0.5. 3.3 Ablation Study: MHD Loss Components We evaluated the contribution of each loss term on the Fluo-N2DH-GOWT1 and Fluo-C2DL-MSC datasets by selectively enabling or disabling individual components of the total loss. As shown in Table 1 , using both MHD terms ( ℒ LMHD \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMHD}} and ℒ RMHD \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RMHD}} ) consistently yields the highest SEG scores, confirming their importance for enforcing accurate boundary alignment and improving instance separation.
